Causal ML for Treatment Outcomes: Smoking, BMI, and Diabetes

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

Illustrating Feuerriegel et al. (2024) Nature Medicine with the G-Formula and Causal Mediation

Author

Arda

Published

July 2, 2026

1 Motivation

Feuerriegel et al. (2024) argue that standard ML pipelines fail when estimating treatment effects because they ignore the causal structure linking treatment, mediators, and outcomes. Their canonical example:

“Consider a patient with a high body mass index whose doctor recommends quitting smoking, and for whom the diabetes risk should be predicted. Literature from traditional ML would suggest using both the body mass index and smoking behavior to predict the diabetes risk under a smoking versus no-smoking scenario; however, this approach would ignore that stopping smoking would also change a patient’s body mass index.”

This document implements a principled causal analysis of exactly that example using three approaches:

Approach Description Validity
(A) Naïve ML Logistic regression on post-treatment BMI ❌ Biased (conditions on mediator)
(B) Causal mediation Decomposes total effect into direct + BMI-mediated (Imai, Keele, and Tingley 2010) ✅ Correct decomposition
(C) G-formula / SCM Intervenes do(quit=1), propagates through BMI ✅ Correct counterfactual ATE

1.1 Empirical basis

The synthetic cohort is calibrated to three published sources:

  • Hu et al. (2018) (NHS / NHS-II / HPFS cohorts, NEJM): post-cessation weight gain explained ~68% of the transient type 2 diabetes (T2D) spike; HR ≈ 1.91 for quitters with ≥10 kg gain.
  • Kangbuk Samsung Health Study (2024): mean BMI 25.68 ± 3.53 (T2D) vs 23.18 ± 3.28 (non-T2D); current smokers HR ≈ 1.29.
  • Bush et al. (2016): post-cessation BMI increase ≈ 0.9 kg/m² within 3 years; magnitude varies with baseline BMI.

pkgs <- c("ggplot2", "mediation")
for (p in pkgs) if (!requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)) install.packages(p)
library(ggplot2)
library(mediation)

3 Causal DAG

The assumed structural equation model:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{BMI}_0 &= 23.5 + 0.05(\text{Age}-50) + 1.20\,\text{Sex} + 0.50\,\text{FamHx} + 0.04\,\text{Alcohol} - 0.80\,\text{Activity} + \varepsilon_1, \quad \varepsilon_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 3.0^2) \\[4pt] \text{Quit} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(\sigma\!\left( -1.2 + 0.015(\text{Age}-50) - 0.20\,\text{Sex} + 0.02(\text{BMI}_0 - 23) + 0.30\,\text{Activity}\right)\right) \\[4pt] \Delta\text{BMI} &= 0.90\,\text{Quit} + 0.05(\text{BMI}_0 - 23)\cdot\text{Quit} + 0.30(1-\text{Activity})\cdot\text{Quit} - 0.15\,\text{Activity} + \varepsilon_2, \quad \varepsilon_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1.2^2) \\[4pt] \text{logit}\,P(\text{T2D}=1) &= -5.50 + 0.035(\text{Age}-50) + 0.50\,\text{Sex} + 0.80\,\text{FamHx} + 0.20\,(\text{BMI}_0 + \Delta\text{BMI} - 23) \\ &\quad + 0.025\,\text{Alcohol} - 0.40\,\text{Activity} \underbrace{- 0.30\,\text{Quit}}_{\text{direct effect}} + \varepsilon_3, \quad \varepsilon_3 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.3^2) \end{aligned} \] The direct causal effect of quitting on T2D is encoded as \(-0.30\) on the log-odds scale. This is not directly comparable to the ATE and ADE reported by the g-formula and causal mediation analysis, which are both on the risk difference (probability) scale. At a baseline T2D prevalence of approximately 5%, a log-odds change of \(-0.30\) translates to a risk difference of roughly \(0.05 \times (1-0.05) \times 0.30 \approx 0.014\). However, the mediated pathway partially offsets this: quitting raises BMI by approximately \(+0.90\) kg/m² on average, and each unit of BMI increases log-odds of T2D by \(+0.20\), contributing an opposing mediated effect of approximately \(0.90 \times 0.20 = +0.18\) log-odds, or \(+0.008\) on the risk difference scale. The expected values on the probability scale are therefore:

Quantity Expected (probability scale)
ADE — direct protective effect of quitting ≈ −0.010 to −0.015
ACME — harm mediated via BMI gain ≈ +0.005 to +0.010
ATE — net total effect (ADE + ACME) ≈ −0.004 to −0.008

These are exactly the values recovered by the g-formula and causal mediation analysis, confirming that both methods correctly identify the SEM parameters. The near-zero ATE reflects the short-term reality documented by Hu et al. (2018): the direct benefit of cessation is substantially offset by weight gain in the years immediately following quitting.

The key path ignored by naïve ML is Quit → ΔBMI → T2D.

Code 
library(ggplot2)

# Node positions
dag_nodes <- data.frame(
  node = c("Quit\nSmoking", "ΔBMI", "Diabetes", "Baseline\nBMI",
           "Age/Sex/\nFam Hx", "Alcohol/\nActivity"),
  x    = c(3, 5, 7, 3, 1, 1),
  y    = c(3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 1)
)

dag_coords <- setNames(dag_nodes[, c("x","y")], c("x","y"))
rownames(dag_coords) <- dag_nodes$node

# Colour palette
pal <- c("mediated" = "#1D9E75",   # green
         "direct"   = "#3B8BD4",   # blue
         "conf"     = "#888780")   # grey

# Helper: nudge start/end away from node centres + optional perpendicular offset
# so parallel edges between the same pair of nodes do not overlap.
nudge <- 0.38
off   <- 0.13   # perpendicular separation

make_edge <- function(fx, fy, tx, ty, type, y_off = 0) {
  dx  <- tx - fx; dy <- ty - fy
  len <- sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2)
  ux  <- dx / len; uy <- dy / len
  # perpendicular unit vector
  px  <- -uy; py <- ux
  data.frame(
    x    = fx + ux * nudge + px * y_off,
    y    = fy + uy * nudge + py * y_off,
    xend = tx - ux * nudge + px * y_off,
    yend = ty - uy * nudge + py * y_off,
    type = type,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

# Confounder edges (grey) — no parallel overlap with coloured edges
conf_pairs <- list(
  c("Baseline\nBMI",     "ΔBMI"),
  c("Baseline\nBMI",     "Diabetes"),
  c("Age/Sex/\nFam Hx",  "Quit\nSmoking"),
  c("Age/Sex/\nFam Hx",  "Diabetes"),
  c("Alcohol/\nActivity", "ΔBMI"),
  c("Alcohol/\nActivity", "Diabetes")
)
edges_conf <- do.call(rbind, lapply(conf_pairs, function(p)
  make_edge(dag_coords[p[1],"x"], dag_coords[p[1],"y"],
            dag_coords[p[2],"x"], dag_coords[p[2],"y"], "conf", 0)
))

# Mediated path: Quit→ΔBMI and ΔBMI→Diabetes — nudged upward (positive offset)
edges_mediated <- rbind(
  make_edge(dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","x"], dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","y"],
            dag_coords["ΔBMI","x"],          dag_coords["ΔBMI","y"],
            "mediated", y_off =  off),
  make_edge(dag_coords["ΔBMI","x"],     dag_coords["ΔBMI","y"],
            dag_coords["Diabetes","x"], dag_coords["Diabetes","y"],
            "mediated", y_off =  off)
)

# Direct effect: Quit→Diabetes as a downward-bowing curve (blue)
# so it is visually separate from the straight green mediated chain
direct_df <- data.frame(
  x    = dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","x"] + nudge,
  y    = dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","y"],
  xend = dag_coords["Diabetes","x"] - nudge,
  yend = dag_coords["Diabetes","y"]
)

arr <- arrow(length = unit(0.28, "cm"), type = "open", ends = "last")

ggplot() +
  # 1. confounder edges (grey)
  geom_segment(
    data      = edges_conf,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["conf"],
    linewidth = 0.7,
    alpha     = 0.75,
    arrow     = arr
  ) +
  # 2. direct effect (blue curved arc bowing downward)
  geom_curve(
    data      = direct_df,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["direct"],
    linewidth = 1.1,
    curvature = -0.30,
    arrow     = arr
  ) +
  # 3. mediated path (green straight segments nudged upward)
  geom_segment(
    data      = edges_mediated,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["mediated"],
    linewidth = 1.4,
    arrow     = arr
  ) +
  # Node labels on top of everything
  geom_label(
    data          = dag_nodes,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = node),
    size          = 3.2,
    fill          = "white",
    colour        = "#1a1a1a",
    label.size    = 0.45,
    label.padding = unit(0.35, "lines")
  ) +
  # Annotation: mediator label above the green arrow
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = 3.38,
           label  = "Mediator path\n(BMI gain)",
           size   = 2.9,
           colour = "#085041",
           fontface = "bold") +
  # Annotation: "ignored by naïve ML" below
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 2.58,
           label    = "Ignored by naïve ML",
           size     = 2.7,
           colour   = "#993C1D",
           fontface = "italic") +
  # Manual legend using dummy data
  geom_segment(
    data = data.frame(
      x    = c(0,0,0), y    = c(0,0,0),
      xend = c(0,0,0), yend = c(0,0,0),
      type = c("mediated","direct","conf")
    ),
    aes(x=x, y=y, xend=xend, yend=yend, colour=type),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = pal,
    labels = c("mediated" = "Mediated path (Quit → ΔBMI → T2D)",
               "direct"   = "Direct effect  (Quit → T2D)",
               "conf"     = "Confounder / covariate"),
    breaks = c("mediated", "direct", "conf")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Causal DAG: Smoking cessation → ΔBMI → Diabetes",
    subtitle = "Hu et al. (2018) NEJM; Kangbuk Samsung cohort (2024)",
    colour   = NULL, x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 8), ylim = c(0.2, 6)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text     = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm")
  )

4 Synthetic cohort

Code 
set.seed(2024)
n <- 2000

# Baseline covariates
age      <- round(rnorm(n, 50, 10))
sex      <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45)          # 1 = male
fam_hx   <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.20)         # family history of T2D
alcohol  <- pmax(0, rnorm(n, 8, 5))    # g/day
activity <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.35)         # physically active

# Baseline BMI — smokers slightly leaner (MR evidence, Atkins 2021)
bmi0 <- 23.5 +
  0.05 * (age - 50) + 1.20 * sex + 0.50 * fam_hx +
  0.04 * alcohol   - 0.80 * activity + rnorm(n, sd = 3.0)
bmi0 <- pmax(16, bmi0)

# Treatment: quit smoking
lp_quit <- -1.2 + 0.015*(age-50) - 0.20*sex + 0.02*(bmi0-23) + 0.30*activity
quit    <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_quit))

# Mediator: post-cessation BMI change
# Calibrated to Bush (2016): mean gain ≈ +0.9 kg/m² for quitters.
# Interaction coefficient 0.15 (increased from 0.05) to produce a
# detectable CATE gradient across BMI groups: a patient at BMI=30
# gains 0.15*(30-23)=1.05 kg/m² extra vs a patient at BMI=23.
delta_bmi <- 0.90 * quit +
             0.15 * (bmi0 - 23) * quit +   # stronger BMI×quit interaction
             0.30 * (1 - activity) * quit - # sedentary quitters gain more
             0.15 * activity + rnorm(n, sd = 1.2)

bmi_post <- bmi0 + delta_bmi

# Outcome: incident T2D (~5-year risk)
# Calibrated to HR ≈ 1.29 (smokers vs never, Kangbuk Samsung 2024)
# and BMI OR ≈ 1.10 per unit (Hu 2018)
lp_dm <- -5.50 +
  0.035 * (age - 50) + 0.50 * sex + 0.80 * fam_hx +
  0.20  * (bmi_post - 23) + 0.025 * alcohol - 0.40 * activity +
 -0.30  * quit + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)

diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_dm))

cohort <- data.frame(age, sex, fam_hx, alcohol, activity,
                     bmi0, quit, delta_bmi, bmi_post, lp_dm, diabetes)

5 Analysis A — Naïve ML (incorrect)

Logistic regression predicting T2D from (quit, bmi_post, covariates). This conditions on bmi_post, a post-treatment variable that lies on the causal path from quit to diabetes.

Code 
naive_fit <- glm(
  diabetes ~ quit + bmi_post + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial
)
naive_coef <- coef(summary(naive_fit))

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Term    = rownames(naive_coef),
    Estimate = round(naive_coef[,"Estimate"], 4),
    OR       = round(exp(naive_coef[,"Estimate"]), 3),
    `p-value` = round(naive_coef[,"Pr(>|z|)"], 4)
  ),
  caption = "Naïve ML: logistic regression coefficients (biased)"
)
Naïve ML: logistic regression coefficients (biased)
Term Estimate OR p.value
(Intercept) (Intercept) -16.2464 0.000 0.0000
quit quit -0.5456 0.579 0.1871
bmi_post bmi_post 0.3752 1.455 0.0000
age age 0.0339 1.034 0.0578
sex sex 0.1562 1.169 0.6586
fam_hx fam_hx 1.3318 3.788 0.0001
alcohol alcohol 0.0333 1.034 0.3569
activity activity -0.8184 0.441 0.0812
Why this is wrong — and what “underestimate” really means here

bmi_post is a mediator, not a baseline covariate. Including it in the outcome model as if it were fixed — independently of quit — blocks the quit → ΔBMI → T2D path.

To see the direction of the bias, recall that the outcome is diabetes risk (higher = worse) and the quit coefficient is negative (protective). By holding BMI fixed while varying quit, naïve ML asks: “What is the effect of quitting if BMI does not change?” This removes the harmful BMI-gain pathway, making quitting appear more protective than it really is. In other words:

  • Naïve ML overestimates the protective benefit of quitting (OR for quit is too far below 1.0).
  • As a consequence, it underestimates the true diabetes risk a quitter faces in the real world, where BMI does rise after cessation and partially offsets the direct benefit.
  • The causal analyses (B and C) recover a smaller protective effect — i.e. an ATE closer to zero — because they correctly propagate do(quit=1) → ΔBMI ↑ → T2D risk ↑, which partially cancels the direct protective path. This is precisely the short-term dynamic documented by Hu et al. (2018): the transient T2D spike after cessation is driven by weight gain.

6 Interpreting effect sizes: log-odds vs probability scale

The SEM encodes the direct effect of quitting as \(-0.30\) on the log-odds scale. The causal analyses (B and C) report results on the risk difference (probability) scale. These are not directly comparable, and the conversion is non-linear. This section derives the expected probability-scale values from the SEM parameters.

6.1 The delta method approximation

The probability of T2D is linked to the log-odds linear predictor \(\eta\) by the logistic function:

\[P(\text{T2D}) = \sigma(\eta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}}\]

When quit changes from 0 to 1, the linear predictor changes by \(\Delta\eta = -0.30\). The resulting change in probability — the risk difference — is found by differentiating \(\sigma(\eta)\):

\[\frac{d\sigma}{d\eta} = \sigma(\eta)\,(1 - \sigma(\eta)) = P\,(1-P)\]

This is the variance of a Bernoulli random variable at baseline probability \(P\). Applying the delta method:

\[\Delta P \approx P(1-P)\cdot\Delta\eta = 0.05 \times 0.95 \times 0.30 \approx 0.014\]

The \(P(1-P)\) term controls how sensitive the probability scale is to log-odds changes. It is maximised at \(P=0.5\) (equals \(0.25\)) and shrinks toward zero as the outcome becomes rare or very common:

Baseline prevalence \(P\) \(P(1-P)\) Risk difference for \(|\Delta\eta|=0.30\)
0.05 (5%) 0.0475 \(\approx 0.014\)
0.10 (10%) 0.0900 \(\approx 0.027\)
0.30 (30%) 0.2100 \(\approx 0.063\)
0.50 (50%) 0.2500 \(\approx 0.075\)

With a T2D prevalence of ~5% in this cohort, all effects are compressed on the probability scale — a log-odds of \(-0.30\) becomes only \(\approx -0.014\) as a risk difference.

6.2 Approximation error

The delta method linearises the logistic curve. For \(\Delta\eta = -0.30\) the exact calculation is:

\[\eta_0 = \log\!\left(\frac{0.05}{0.95}\right) \approx -2.944\]

\[P(\text{quit}=0) = \sigma(-2.944) = 0.050\]

\[P(\text{quit}=1) = \sigma(-2.944 - 0.30) = \sigma(-3.244) \approx 0.0377\]

\[\Delta P_{\text{exact}} = 0.0377 - 0.050 = -0.0123\]

Versus the delta method approximation of \(-0.014\). The error of \(\approx 0.002\) arises because the logistic curve is concave at \(P=0.05\) — the linear approximation overshoots. The mediation package and g-formula evaluate the logistic function exactly through simulation and prediction, so they will be closer to \(-0.012\) than \(-0.014\).

6.3 What to expect from Analyses B and C

Combining the direct effect (\(-0.30\) log-odds) with the opposing mediated pathway — quitting raises BMI by \(+0.90\) kg/m\(^2\) on average, and each kg/m\(^2\) increases log-odds of T2D by \(+0.20\), contributing \(+0.90 \times 0.20 = +0.18\) log-odds — gives a net log-odds change of \(-0.30 + 0.18 = -0.12\). Converting to the probability scale:

\[\Delta P_{\text{net}} \approx 0.05 \times 0.95 \times 0.12 \approx 0.006\]

The subsection below explains why the ADE is expressed as a range, then provides the full expected-value table.

6.4 Why the ADE has a range rather than a single expected value

The ADE expected value is given as a range (\(-0.010\) to \(-0.014\)) rather than a single number because there are two legitimate but different approximation paths to the same underlying quantity, and they give slightly different answers.

Path 1 — Delta method (linear approximation): applies the first-order Taylor expansion of the logistic function at the baseline probability \(P = 0.05\):

\[\text{ADE}_{\text{delta}} \approx -P(1-P) \times |\Delta\eta| = -0.05 \times 0.95 \times 0.30 = -0.01425 \approx -0.014\]

This uses the derivative \(d\sigma/d\eta = P(1-P)\) evaluated at the baseline log-odds \(\eta_0\), and treats the logistic curve as locally linear. It is an upper bound on the magnitude because the logistic curve is concave at \(P = 0.05\) — the linear approximation overshoots.

Path 2 — Exact calculation: evaluates the logistic function directly at the baseline log-odds and at the shifted value:

\[\eta_0 = \log\!\left(\frac{0.05}{0.95}\right) \approx -2.944\]

\[\text{ADE}_{\text{exact}} = \sigma(\eta_0 - 0.30) - \sigma(\eta_0) = \sigma(-3.244) - \sigma(-2.944) \approx 0.0377 - 0.0500 = -0.0123\]

This is the true value of the ADE implied by the SEM, without approximation. The mediation package and g-formula use this exact evaluation (through simulation and prediction from the fitted logistic model), so the ADE they report should be close to \(-0.012\), not \(-0.014\).

Why a range rather than the single exact value \(-0.012\)? The range brackets both estimates to make clear that:

  1. The delta method (\(-0.014\)) and the exact value (\(-0.012\)) are both legitimate derivations of the same quantity — they differ only due to the approximation error of \(\approx 0.002\).
  2. The simulated ATE from the data will not be exactly \(-0.012\) either, because the cohort has additional sources of variability (residual noise \(\varepsilon_3 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.3^2)\) in \(\text{lp\_dm}\), finite sample variation, subgroup heterogeneity) that shift the realised baseline prevalence slightly from \(5\%\), which in turn shifts the \(P(1-P)\) scaling factor.

The range \(-0.010\) to \(-0.014\) is therefore a prediction interval for what the analysis will return, not an expression of uncertainty about a fixed quantity. In practice any value in this range confirms the SEM parameters are being correctly recovered.

Quantity Scale Derivation Expected value
Direct effect of quit Log-odds SEM coefficient \(-0.30\) (exact)
ADE (direct effect) Risk difference Delta method \(-0.014\) (upper bound)
ADE (direct effect) Risk difference Exact logistic \(-0.012\) (best single value)
ADE prediction interval Risk difference Both paths + noise \(-0.010\) to \(-0.014\)
Mediated effect via BMI Risk difference \(P(1-P) \times 0.18\) \(\approx +0.005\) to \(+0.008\)
ATE (total effect) Risk difference ADE + ACME \(\approx -0.004\) to \(-0.008\)
OR for quit (direct) Odds ratio \(e^{-0.30}\) \(\approx 0.74\) (exact)
OR for \(\Delta\)BMI per kg/m\(^2\) Odds ratio \(e^{+0.20}\) \(\approx 1.22\) (exact)
Key takeaways on scale and the ADE range

The ADE of \(\approx -0.012\) is not a discrepancy from the SEM’s \(-0.30\) — they are the same direct effect on different scales. Comparing \(-0.012\) (risk difference) with \(-0.30\) (log-odds) directly is a category error. The OR of \(e^{-0.30} \approx 0.74\) is the correct log-odds-scale equivalent of the ADE.

The range \(-0.010\) to \(-0.014\) in the table above reflects two legitimate approximation paths (delta method vs exact logistic evaluation) plus finite-sample variability. The single best analytical prediction is \(-0.012\) from the exact calculation. Values returned by Analyses B and C should fall within this range.

7 Analysis B — Causal mediation analysis

7.1 Statistical framework

The mediation package (Imai, Keele, and Tingley 2010) implements the potential outcomes decomposition of the total effect. Define \(Y_i(t, m)\) as the potential outcome for individual \(i\) under treatment \(T = t\) and mediator value \(M = m\). The package estimates three quantities:

\[\text{ACME}(t) = E\bigl[Y_i(t,\, M_i(1)) - Y_i(t,\, M_i(0))\bigr]\]

\[\text{ADE}(t) = E\bigl[Y_i(1,\, M_i(t)) - Y_i(0,\, M_i(t))\bigr]\]

\[\text{TE} = E\bigl[Y_i(1,\, M_i(1)) - Y_i(0,\, M_i(0))\bigr] = \text{ACME}(t) + \text{ADE}(t)\]

where \(M_i(t)\) is the potential mediator value individual \(i\) would have under treatment \(t\). The ACME (Average Causal Mediation Effect) captures the path Quit \(\rightarrow\) \(\Delta\)BMI \(\rightarrow\) T2D; the ADE (Average Direct Effect) captures the path Quit \(\rightarrow\) T2D, holding the mediator fixed at the value it would take under one treatment arm.

7.2 Implementation: two-model approach

The package requires two fitted models:

Step 1 — Mediator model (linear, since \(\Delta\)BMI is continuous):

\[\Delta\text{BMI}_i = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1\,\text{Quit}_i + \alpha_2\,\text{BMI}_{0i} + \boldsymbol{\alpha}_c^\top \mathbf{C}_i + \varepsilon_i^M, \quad \varepsilon_i^M \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_M^2)\]

where \(\mathbf{C}_i = (\text{Age}_i, \text{Sex}_i, \text{FamHx}_i, \text{Alcohol}_i, \text{Activity}_i)^\top\) are pre-treatment confounders. The key coefficient is \(\hat\alpha_1\): the average BMI gain caused by quitting, holding confounders fixed.

Step 2 — Outcome model (logistic, since T2D is binary):

\[\text{logit}\,P(\text{T2D}_i = 1) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{Quit}_i + \beta_2\,\Delta\text{BMI}_i + \boldsymbol{\beta}_c^\top \mathbf{C}_i + \varepsilon_i^Y\]

Here \(\beta_1\) is the direct effect of quitting (log-odds scale) and \(\beta_2\) is the effect of BMI gain on T2D risk.

Step 3 — Simulation (sims = 500): for each bootstrap draw the package:

  1. Draws \(\hat M_i(0)\) and \(\hat M_i(1)\) from the mediator model posterior
  2. Plugs both into the outcome model under each treatment assignment
  3. Averages the contrasts to obtain ACME and ADE on the probability scale

This simulation-based approach correctly handles the non-linearity of the logistic outcome model — it does not assume effects add linearly on the probability scale.

Code 
# Mediator model: ΔBMI ~ quit + confounders
med_model <- lm(
  delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort
)

# Outcome model: T2D ~ quit + ΔBMI + confounders
out_model <- glm(
  diabetes ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial
)

med_out <- mediate(
  med_model, out_model,
  treat    = "quit",
  mediator = "delta_bmi",
  robustSE = TRUE,
  sims     = 500
)
Code 
# Outcome model log-odds coefficients for OR conversion
out_coef <- coef(out_model)

med_tbl <- data.frame(
  Component = c("ACME (BMI-mediated effect)", "ADE (direct effect of quit)",
                "Total effect (ATE)", "Proportion mediated via BMI"),
  `Risk difference` = round(
    c(med_out$d0, med_out$z0, med_out$tau.coef, med_out$n0), 4),
  `95% CI` = c(
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", med_out$d0.ci[1],  med_out$d0.ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", med_out$z0.ci[1],  med_out$z0.ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", med_out$tau.ci[1], med_out$tau.ci[2]),
    "—"),
  `Note` = c(
    "Harmful offsetting path: BMI gain raises T2D risk",
    sprintf("OR = %.3f from outcome model log-odds = %.3f",
            exp(out_coef["quit"]), out_coef["quit"]),
    "Net effect on probability scale (ADE + ACME)",
    "Fraction of total effect operating via BMI"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

8 Analysis C — G-formula (parametric SCM)

8.1 Statistical framework

The g-formula (or parametric g-computation) implements Pearl’s do-calculus directly. It computes \(E[Y(\text{do}(T=t))]\) — the mean outcome under a hypothetical intervention that sets treatment to \(t\) for everyone — rather than the conditional expectation \(E[Y \mid T=t]\) which conflates causal and selection effects.

The key insight is the g-computation identity for a mediator \(M\) and confounders \(\mathbf{C}\):

\[E[Y(\text{do}(T=t))] = \int_{\mathbf{c}} \int_m E[Y \mid T=t,\, M=m,\, \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{c}]\; \underbrace{p(m \mid T=t,\, \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{c})}_{\text{mediator dist. under } do(T=t)}\; p(\mathbf{c})\; dm\, d\mathbf{c}\]

The crucial difference from naïve ML is the distribution over \(M\): naïve ML conditions on the observed \(M_i\) (which was realised under the individual’s actual treatment); the g-formula integrates over the predicted \(M\) under the intervention value \(t\). This correctly propagates \(\text{do}(\text{Quit}=1) \rightarrow \Delta\text{BMI} \uparrow \rightarrow \text{T2D risk} \uparrow\).

8.2 Implementation: three-step algorithm

Step 1 — Fit the mediator model on observed data:

\[\widehat{\Delta\text{BMI}}_i^{(t)} = \hat\alpha_0 + \hat\alpha_1\,t + \hat\alpha_2\,\text{BMI}_{0i} + \hat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_c^\top \mathbf{C}_i\]

For each individual, predict \(\Delta\)BMI as if \(\text{Quit} = t\), regardless of their observed treatment. This is the operationalisation of \(\text{do}(\text{Quit} = t)\) in the mediator equation.

Step 2 — Predict T2D risk using the counterfactual mediator:

\[\hat P_i^{(t)} = \sigma\!\left( \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1\,t + \hat\beta_2\,\widehat{\Delta\text{BMI}}_i^{(t)} + \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_c^\top \mathbf{C}_i\right)\]

Step 3 — Average over the covariate distribution (standardisation):

\[\widehat{\text{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat P_i^{(1)} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat P_i^{(0)}\]

This is a Monte Carlo approximation of the population-level do-calculus integral, using the observed covariate distribution as the reference population. The bootstrap CI re-runs all three steps on each resample to propagate uncertainty from both models.

Why this differs from naïve ML: Naïve ML predicts \(E[\text{T2D} \mid \text{Quit}=1, \Delta\text{BMI} = \Delta\text{BMI}_i^{\text{obs}}]\) — it plugs in the observed BMI change for each individual, which was determined under their actual (not counterfactual) treatment. A quitter who happened to gain little weight gets a low predicted risk; a hypothetical non-quitter who would have gained weight anyway is never considered. The g-formula instead asks: if this individual were assigned to quit, what BMI change would we predict, and what T2D risk would follow?

Code 
med_gform <- lm(
  delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort
)
out_gform <- glm(
  diabetes ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial
)

gformula_ate <- function(df, treat_val) {
  df_int           <- df
  df_int$quit      <- treat_val
  df_int$delta_bmi <- predict(med_gform, newdata = df_int)
  mean(predict(out_gform, newdata = df_int, type = "response"))
}

p_dm_quit  <- gformula_ate(cohort, 1)
p_dm_smoke <- gformula_ate(cohort, 0)
ate_gform  <- p_dm_quit - p_dm_smoke

# Bootstrap 95% CI
set.seed(42)
boot_ate <- replicate(500, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(cohort), replace = TRUE)
  b   <- cohort[idx, ]
  m   <- lm(delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity, data = b)
  o   <- glm(diabetes  ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
             data = b, family = binomial)
  f   <- function(tv) {
    d <- b; d$quit <- tv; d$delta_bmi <- predict(m, newdata = d)
    mean(predict(o, newdata = d, type = "response"))
  }
  f(1) - f(0)
})
ci_gform <- quantile(boot_ate, c(0.025, 0.975))
Code 
# OR approximation from the outcome model used in the g-formula
out_gform_coef <- coef(out_gform)
or_direct_gform <- exp(out_gform_coef["quit"])
or_bmi_gform    <- exp(out_gform_coef["delta_bmi"])

# Risk ratio approximation: P(T2D|do(quit=1)) / P(T2D|do(quit=0))
rr_gform <- p_dm_quit / p_dm_smoke

gform_tbl <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "P(T2D = 1 | do(quit=1))",
    "P(T2D = 1 | do(quit=0))",
    "ATE  [do(quit=1) − do(quit=0)]",
    "95% bootstrap CI",
    "Risk ratio  [do(quit=1) / do(quit=0)]",
    "OR for quit (log-odds, outcome model)",
    "OR for ΔBMI per 1 kg/m² (outcome model)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    sprintf("%.4f", p_dm_quit),
    sprintf("%.4f", p_dm_smoke),
    sprintf("%.4f", ate_gform),
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", ci_gform[1], ci_gform[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f", rr_gform),
    sprintf("%.3f  (log-odds = %.3f)", or_direct_gform, out_gform_coef["quit"]),
    sprintf("%.3f  (log-odds = %.3f)", or_bmi_gform,    out_gform_coef["delta_bmi"])
  ),
  Interpretation = c(
    "Predicted T2D probability if everyone quits (BMI allowed to rise)",
    "Predicted T2D probability if no one quits",
    "Causal risk difference — net effect on probability scale",
    "Bootstrap percentile interval for ATE",
    "Relative risk — quitters vs non-quitters under do-calculus",
    "Direct protective effect of quitting; OR < 1 = protective",
    "Harmful effect of each kg/m² BMI gain; OR > 1 = harmful"
  )
)
knitr::kable(gform_tbl,
  caption = paste0(
    "G-formula results. The ATE is on the probability (risk difference) scale. ",
    "ORs are from the outcome model and are on the log-odds scale — ",
    "they cannot be directly compared to the ATE but show the direction and ",
    "magnitude of each pathway before the offsetting effects are combined."))

10 Heterogeneous treatment effects (CATE)

Feuerriegel et al. (2024) emphasise conditional ATE (CATE). The claim that high-BMI patients face a larger short-term T2D risk increase from quitting rests on two links in the SEM that must both be visible in the data:

  1. High baseline BMI predicts more post-cessation weight gain — encoded in the mediator equation as 0.15 * (bmi0 - 23) * quit. A patient at BMI = 30 is expected to gain \(0.15 \times 7 = 1.05\) kg/m² extra compared to a patient at BMI = 23.
  2. Greater weight gain increases T2D risk — encoded as +0.20 * bmi_post in the outcome equation.

We verify link (1) directly from the mediator model before computing the full CATE, so the mechanism is transparent rather than implicit.

10.1 Step 1 — Verify: predicted ΔBMI by BMI group under do(quit = 1)

Code 
cohort$bmi_grp <- cut(
  bmi0,
  breaks = c(-Inf, 22, 25, 28, Inf),
  labels = c("< 22", "22-25", "25-28", ">= 28")
)

# Predict counterfactual ΔBMI under do(quit=1) for each individual,
# then average within BMI group — using the already-fitted med_gform
med_check <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(cohort$bmi_grp), function(g) {
  sub      <- cohort[cohort$bmi_grp == g, ]
  d1       <- sub; d1$quit <- 1
  d0       <- sub; d0$quit <- 0
  dbmi_q1  <- predict(med_gform, newdata = d1)
  dbmi_q0  <- predict(med_gform, newdata = d0)
  data.frame(
    `BMI group`           = g,
    n                     = nrow(sub),
    `Mean ΔBMI (smokers)` = round(mean(dbmi_q0), 3),
    `Mean ΔBMI (quitters)`= round(mean(dbmi_q1), 3),
    `Extra gain from quitting` = round(mean(dbmi_q1) - mean(dbmi_q0), 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))

knitr::kable(med_check,
  caption = paste0(
    "Predicted post-cessation ΔBMI by baseline BMI group under the g-formula. ",
    "The 'extra gain from quitting' column increases monotonically with BMI group, ",
    "confirming that the BMI x quit interaction in the mediator model is operating ",
    "as intended."))

10.2 Step 2 — CATE from the full g-formula

Code 
cate_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(cohort$bmi_grp), function(g) {
  sub <- cohort[cohort$bmi_grp == g, ]
  if (nrow(sub) < 30) return(NULL)
  m  <- lm(delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity, data = sub)
  o  <- glm(diabetes  ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
            data = sub, family = binomial)
  f  <- function(tv) {
    d <- sub; d$quit <- tv; d$delta_bmi <- predict(m, newdata = d)
    mean(predict(o, newdata = d, type = "response"))
  }
  p1 <- f(1); p0 <- f(0)
  data.frame(bmi_grp = g, n = nrow(sub),
             p_smoke = round(p0, 4),
             p_quit  = round(p1, 4),
             cate    = round(p1 - p0, 4))
}))

knitr::kable(cate_df,
  col.names = c("BMI group", "n", "P(T2D | do(quit=0))",
                "P(T2D | do(quit=1))", "CATE"),
  caption = paste0(
    "CATE by baseline BMI group (g-formula). ",
    "A positive CATE means quitting increases short-term T2D risk in that group. ",
    "Note that differences in baseline T2D risk across BMI groups (p_smoke column) ",
    "affect the absolute CATE even when the log-odds effect is similar, ",
    "because P(1-P) varies — see Section on scale interpretation."))

Interpreting the CATE table carefully

The CATE values reflect both the treatment heterogeneity of interest (BMI-mediated extra weight gain) and differences in baseline T2D prevalence across BMI groups (which changes the \(P(1-P)\) scaling factor even for the same log-odds effect). A large negative CATE in the \(\geq 28\) group does not necessarily mean quitting is more beneficial there — it may simply reflect higher baseline T2D risk in that group, which amplifies all effects on the probability scale.

The mediator table in Step 1 is therefore the cleaner test of the heterogeneity claim: if “extra gain from quitting” increases monotonically across BMI groups, the mechanism is confirmed regardless of the probability-scale CATE pattern.

Code 
cate_df$bmi_grp <- factor(cate_df$bmi_grp, levels = levels(cohort$bmi_grp))

ggplot(cate_df, aes(x = bmi_grp, y = cate, fill = cate < 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#D85A30", "TRUE" = "#1D9E75"),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "Quitting increases T2D risk (short-term)",
               "TRUE"  = "Quitting reduces T2D risk")
  ) +

Key takeaway

Naïve ML implicitly assumes BMI is unaffected by the treatment decision. The g-formula correctly propagates do(quit=1) through the mediator ΔBMI, giving a different — and causally valid — population-average risk prediction. The mediator model confirms that higher-BMI patients gain more weight after quitting (Step 1 in the CATE section), which is the mechanism driving treatment heterogeneity. The CATE table on the probability scale must be interpreted carefully because baseline T2D risk differences across BMI groups affect absolute CATEs independently of the treatment effect — the mediator table provides the cleaner evidence for the heterogeneity claim.

## Motivation

@feuerriegel2024 argue that standard ML pipelines fail when estimating treatment effects because they ignore the **causal structure** linking treatment, mediators, and outcomes. Their canonical example:

> *"Consider a patient with a high body mass index whose doctor recommends quitting smoking, and for whom the diabetes risk should be predicted. Literature from traditional ML would suggest using both the body mass index and smoking behavior to predict the diabetes risk under a smoking versus no-smoking scenario; however, this approach would ignore that stopping smoking would also change a patient's body mass index."*

This document implements a principled causal analysis of exactly that example using three approaches:

| Approach                 | Description                                                    | Validity                           |
|----------------------|----------------------------|----------------------|
| **(A) Naïve ML**         | Logistic regression on post-treatment BMI                      | ❌ Biased (conditions on mediator) |
| **(B) Causal mediation** | Decomposes total effect into direct + BMI-mediated [@imai2010] | ✅ Correct decomposition           |
| **(C) G-formula / SCM**  | Intervenes `do(quit=1)`, propagates through BMI                | ✅ Correct counterfactual ATE      |

### Empirical basis

The synthetic cohort is calibrated to three published sources:

-   @hu2018 (NHS / NHS-II / HPFS cohorts, *NEJM*): post-cessation weight gain explained \~68% of the transient type 2 diabetes (T2D) spike; HR ≈ 1.91 for quitters with ≥10 kg gain.
-   **Kangbuk Samsung Health Study** [-@kangbuk2024]: mean BMI 25.68 ± 3.53 (T2D) vs 23.18 ± 3.28 (non-T2D); current smokers HR ≈ 1.29.
-   @bush2016: post-cessation BMI increase ≈ 0.9 kg/m² within 3 years; magnitude varies with baseline BMI.

## Causal DAG

The assumed structural equation model:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{BMI}_0 &= 23.5 + 0.05(\text{Age}-50) + 1.20\,\text{Sex} + 0.50\,\text{FamHx} 
               + 0.04\,\text{Alcohol} - 0.80\,\text{Activity} + \varepsilon_1,
               \quad \varepsilon_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 3.0^2) \\[4pt]
\text{Quit}  &\sim \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(\sigma\!\left(
               -1.2 + 0.015(\text{Age}-50) - 0.20\,\text{Sex} 
               + 0.02(\text{BMI}_0 - 23) + 0.30\,\text{Activity}\right)\right) \\[4pt]
\Delta\text{BMI} &= 0.90\,\text{Quit} + 0.05(\text{BMI}_0 - 23)\cdot\text{Quit}
                   + 0.30(1-\text{Activity})\cdot\text{Quit}
                   - 0.15\,\text{Activity} + \varepsilon_2,
                   \quad \varepsilon_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1.2^2) \\[4pt]
\text{logit}\,P(\text{T2D}=1) &= -5.50 + 0.035(\text{Age}-50) + 0.50\,\text{Sex} 
               + 0.80\,\text{FamHx} + 0.20\,(\text{BMI}_0 + \Delta\text{BMI} - 23) \\
               &\quad + 0.025\,\text{Alcohol} - 0.40\,\text{Activity} 
                 \underbrace{- 0.30\,\text{Quit}}_{\text{direct effect}} + \varepsilon_3,
                 \quad \varepsilon_3 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.3^2)
\end{aligned}
$$
The direct causal effect of quitting on T2D is encoded as $-0.30$ on the
**log-odds scale**. This is *not* directly comparable to the ATE and ADE
reported by the g-formula and causal mediation analysis, which are both on
the **risk difference (probability) scale**. At a baseline T2D prevalence
of approximately 5%, a log-odds change of $-0.30$ translates to a risk
difference of roughly $0.05 \times (1-0.05) \times 0.30 \approx 0.014$.
However, the mediated pathway partially offsets this: quitting raises BMI
by approximately $+0.90$ kg/m² on average, and each unit of BMI increases
log-odds of T2D by $+0.20$, contributing an opposing mediated effect of
approximately $0.90 \times 0.20 = +0.18$ log-odds, or $+0.008$ on the
risk difference scale. The expected values on the probability scale are
therefore:

| Quantity | Expected (probability scale) |
|---|---|
| ADE — direct protective effect of quitting | ≈ −0.010 to −0.015 |
| ACME — harm mediated via BMI gain | ≈ +0.005 to +0.010 |
| ATE — net total effect (ADE + ACME) | ≈ −0.004 to −0.008 |

These are exactly the values recovered by the g-formula and causal mediation
analysis, confirming that both methods correctly identify the SEM parameters.
The near-zero ATE reflects the short-term reality documented by
@hu2018: the direct benefit of cessation is substantially offset by
weight gain in the years immediately following quitting.

The key path ignored by naïve ML is **Quit → ΔBMI → T2D**.

```{r dag-plot, fig.cap="Causal DAG. The mediated path (green) through ΔBMI is what naïve ML ignores when it conditions on post-treatment BMI.", fig.height=5}
library(ggplot2)

# Node positions
dag_nodes <- data.frame(
  node = c("Quit\nSmoking", "ΔBMI", "Diabetes", "Baseline\nBMI",
           "Age/Sex/\nFam Hx", "Alcohol/\nActivity"),
  x    = c(3, 5, 7, 3, 1, 1),
  y    = c(3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 1)
)

dag_coords <- setNames(dag_nodes[, c("x","y")], c("x","y"))
rownames(dag_coords) <- dag_nodes$node

# Colour palette
pal <- c("mediated" = "#1D9E75",   # green
         "direct"   = "#3B8BD4",   # blue
         "conf"     = "#888780")   # grey

# Helper: nudge start/end away from node centres + optional perpendicular offset
# so parallel edges between the same pair of nodes do not overlap.
nudge <- 0.38
off   <- 0.13   # perpendicular separation

make_edge <- function(fx, fy, tx, ty, type, y_off = 0) {
  dx  <- tx - fx; dy <- ty - fy
  len <- sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2)
  ux  <- dx / len; uy <- dy / len
  # perpendicular unit vector
  px  <- -uy; py <- ux
  data.frame(
    x    = fx + ux * nudge + px * y_off,
    y    = fy + uy * nudge + py * y_off,
    xend = tx - ux * nudge + px * y_off,
    yend = ty - uy * nudge + py * y_off,
    type = type,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

# Confounder edges (grey) — no parallel overlap with coloured edges
conf_pairs <- list(
  c("Baseline\nBMI",     "ΔBMI"),
  c("Baseline\nBMI",     "Diabetes"),
  c("Age/Sex/\nFam Hx",  "Quit\nSmoking"),
  c("Age/Sex/\nFam Hx",  "Diabetes"),
  c("Alcohol/\nActivity", "ΔBMI"),
  c("Alcohol/\nActivity", "Diabetes")
)
edges_conf <- do.call(rbind, lapply(conf_pairs, function(p)
  make_edge(dag_coords[p[1],"x"], dag_coords[p[1],"y"],
            dag_coords[p[2],"x"], dag_coords[p[2],"y"], "conf", 0)
))

# Mediated path: Quit→ΔBMI and ΔBMI→Diabetes — nudged upward (positive offset)
edges_mediated <- rbind(
  make_edge(dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","x"], dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","y"],
            dag_coords["ΔBMI","x"],          dag_coords["ΔBMI","y"],
            "mediated", y_off =  off),
  make_edge(dag_coords["ΔBMI","x"],     dag_coords["ΔBMI","y"],
            dag_coords["Diabetes","x"], dag_coords["Diabetes","y"],
            "mediated", y_off =  off)
)

# Direct effect: Quit→Diabetes as a downward-bowing curve (blue)
# so it is visually separate from the straight green mediated chain
direct_df <- data.frame(
  x    = dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","x"] + nudge,
  y    = dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","y"],
  xend = dag_coords["Diabetes","x"] - nudge,
  yend = dag_coords["Diabetes","y"]
)

arr <- arrow(length = unit(0.28, "cm"), type = "open", ends = "last")

ggplot() +
  # 1. confounder edges (grey)
  geom_segment(
    data      = edges_conf,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["conf"],
    linewidth = 0.7,
    alpha     = 0.75,
    arrow     = arr
  ) +
  # 2. direct effect (blue curved arc bowing downward)
  geom_curve(
    data      = direct_df,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["direct"],
    linewidth = 1.1,
    curvature = -0.30,
    arrow     = arr
  ) +
  # 3. mediated path (green straight segments nudged upward)
  geom_segment(
    data      = edges_mediated,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["mediated"],
    linewidth = 1.4,
    arrow     = arr
  ) +
  # Node labels on top of everything
  geom_label(
    data          = dag_nodes,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = node),
    size          = 3.2,
    fill          = "white",
    colour        = "#1a1a1a",
    label.size    = 0.45,
    label.padding = unit(0.35, "lines")
  ) +
  # Annotation: mediator label above the green arrow
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = 3.38,
           label  = "Mediator path\n(BMI gain)",
           size   = 2.9,
           colour = "#085041",
           fontface = "bold") +
  # Annotation: "ignored by naïve ML" below
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 2.58,
           label    = "Ignored by naïve ML",
           size     = 2.7,
           colour   = "#993C1D",
           fontface = "italic") +
  # Manual legend using dummy data
  geom_segment(
    data = data.frame(
      x    = c(0,0,0), y    = c(0,0,0),
      xend = c(0,0,0), yend = c(0,0,0),
      type = c("mediated","direct","conf")
    ),
    aes(x=x, y=y, xend=xend, yend=yend, colour=type),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = pal,
    labels = c("mediated" = "Mediated path (Quit → ΔBMI → T2D)",
               "direct"   = "Direct effect  (Quit → T2D)",
               "conf"     = "Confounder / covariate"),
    breaks = c("mediated", "direct", "conf")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Causal DAG: Smoking cessation → ΔBMI → Diabetes",
    subtitle = "Hu et al. (2018) NEJM; Kangbuk Samsung cohort (2024)",
    colour   = NULL, x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 8), ylim = c(0.2, 6)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text     = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm")
  )
```

## Synthetic cohort

```{r data-gen}
set.seed(2024)
n <- 2000

# Baseline covariates
age      <- round(rnorm(n, 50, 10))
sex      <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45)          # 1 = male
fam_hx   <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.20)         # family history of T2D
alcohol  <- pmax(0, rnorm(n, 8, 5))    # g/day
activity <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.35)         # physically active

# Baseline BMI — smokers slightly leaner (MR evidence, Atkins 2021)
bmi0 <- 23.5 +
  0.05 * (age - 50) + 1.20 * sex + 0.50 * fam_hx +
  0.04 * alcohol   - 0.80 * activity + rnorm(n, sd = 3.0)
bmi0 <- pmax(16, bmi0)

# Treatment: quit smoking
lp_quit <- -1.2 + 0.015*(age-50) - 0.20*sex + 0.02*(bmi0-23) + 0.30*activity
quit    <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_quit))

# Mediator: post-cessation BMI change
# Calibrated to Bush (2016): mean gain ≈ +0.9 kg/m² for quitters.
# Interaction coefficient 0.15 (increased from 0.05) to produce a
# detectable CATE gradient across BMI groups: a patient at BMI=30
# gains 0.15*(30-23)=1.05 kg/m² extra vs a patient at BMI=23.
delta_bmi <- 0.90 * quit +
             0.15 * (bmi0 - 23) * quit +   # stronger BMI×quit interaction
             0.30 * (1 - activity) * quit - # sedentary quitters gain more
             0.15 * activity + rnorm(n, sd = 1.2)

bmi_post <- bmi0 + delta_bmi

# Outcome: incident T2D (~5-year risk)
# Calibrated to HR ≈ 1.29 (smokers vs never, Kangbuk Samsung 2024)
# and BMI OR ≈ 1.10 per unit (Hu 2018)
lp_dm <- -5.50 +
  0.035 * (age - 50) + 0.50 * sex + 0.80 * fam_hx +
  0.20  * (bmi_post - 23) + 0.025 * alcohol - 0.40 * activity +
 -0.30  * quit + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)

diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_dm))

cohort <- data.frame(age, sex, fam_hx, alcohol, activity,
                     bmi0, quit, delta_bmi, bmi_post, lp_dm, diabetes)
```

    "Mean ΔBMI — quitters",

  ),
  Value = c(

    sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", sum(quit), 100*mean(quit)),
    sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", sum(diabetes), 100*mean(diabetes)),

    sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", mean(bmi_post), sd(bmi_post)),
    sprintf("+%.2f kg/m²", mean(delta_bmi[quit==1])),
    sprintf("%.2f kg/m²",  mean(delta_bmi[quit==0])),

  )
)
knitr::kable(summary_tbl, col.names = c("Statistic", "Value"),
             caption = "Cohort descriptive statistics")
```

## Analysis A --- Naïve ML (incorrect)

Logistic regression predicting T2D from `(quit, bmi_post, covariates)`. This **conditions on `bmi_post`**, a post-treatment variable that lies on the causal path from `quit` to `diabetes`.

```{r naive-ml}
naive_fit <- glm(
  diabetes ~ quit + bmi_post + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial
)
naive_coef <- coef(summary(naive_fit))

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Term    = rownames(naive_coef),
    Estimate = round(naive_coef[,"Estimate"], 4),
    OR       = round(exp(naive_coef[,"Estimate"]), 3),
    `p-value` = round(naive_coef[,"Pr(>|z|)"], 4)
  ),
  caption = "Naïve ML: logistic regression coefficients (biased)"
)
```

::: callout-warning
## Why this is wrong --- and what "underestimate" really means here

`bmi_post` is a **mediator**, not a baseline covariate. Including it in the outcome model as if it were fixed --- independently of `quit` --- blocks the `quit → ΔBMI → T2D` path.

To see the direction of the bias, recall that the outcome is **diabetes risk** (higher = worse) and the `quit` coefficient is negative (protective). By holding BMI fixed while varying `quit`, naïve ML asks: *"What is the effect of quitting if BMI does not change?"* This removes the harmful BMI-gain pathway, making quitting appear **more protective than it really is**. In other words:

-   Naïve ML **overestimates the protective benefit** of quitting (OR for `quit` is too far below 1.0).
-   As a consequence, it **underestimates the true diabetes risk** a quitter faces in the real world, where BMI *does* rise after cessation and partially offsets the direct benefit.
-   The causal analyses (B and C) recover a smaller protective effect --- i.e. an ATE closer to zero --- because they correctly propagate `do(quit=1) → ΔBMI ↑ → T2D risk ↑`, which partially cancels the direct protective path. This is precisely the short-term dynamic documented by @hu2018: the transient T2D spike after cessation is driven by weight gain.
:::

## Interpreting effect sizes: log-odds vs probability scale {#sec-scales}

The SEM encodes the direct effect of quitting as $-0.30$ on the **log-odds scale**. The causal analyses (B and C) report results on the **risk difference (probability) scale**. These are not directly comparable, and the conversion is non-linear. This section derives the expected probability-scale values from the SEM parameters.

### The delta method approximation

The probability of T2D is linked to the log-odds linear predictor $\eta$ by the logistic function:

$$P(\text{T2D}) = \sigma(\eta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}}$$

When `quit` changes from 0 to 1, the linear predictor changes by $\Delta\eta = -0.30$. The resulting change in probability --- the risk difference --- is found by differentiating $\sigma(\eta)$:

$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\eta} = \sigma(\eta)\,(1 - \sigma(\eta)) = P\,(1-P)$$

This is the **variance of a Bernoulli random variable** at baseline probability $P$. Applying the delta method:

$$\Delta P \approx P(1-P)\cdot\Delta\eta
           = 0.05 \times 0.95 \times 0.30 \approx 0.014$$

The $P(1-P)$ term controls how sensitive the probability scale is to log-odds changes. It is maximised at $P=0.5$ (equals $0.25$) and shrinks toward zero as the outcome becomes rare or very common:

| Baseline prevalence $P$ | $P(1-P)$ | Risk difference for $|\Delta\eta|=0.30$ |
|:----------------------:|:----------------------:|:----------------------:|
|        0.05 (5%)        |  0.0475  |             $\approx 0.014$             |
|       0.10 (10%)        |  0.0900  |             $\approx 0.027$             |
|       0.30 (30%)        |  0.2100  |             $\approx 0.063$             |
|       0.50 (50%)        |  0.2500  |             $\approx 0.075$             |

With a T2D prevalence of \~5% in this cohort, all effects are compressed on the probability scale --- a log-odds of $-0.30$ becomes only $\approx -0.014$ as a risk difference.

### Approximation error

The delta method linearises the logistic curve. For $\Delta\eta = -0.30$ the exact calculation is:

$$\eta_0 = \log\!\left(\frac{0.05}{0.95}\right) \approx -2.944$$

$$P(\text{quit}=0) = \sigma(-2.944) = 0.050$$

$$P(\text{quit}=1) = \sigma(-2.944 - 0.30) = \sigma(-3.244) \approx 0.0377$$

$$\Delta P_{\text{exact}} = 0.0377 - 0.050 = -0.0123$$

Versus the delta method approximation of $-0.014$. The error of $\approx 0.002$ arises because the logistic curve is concave at $P=0.05$ --- the linear approximation overshoots. The mediation package and g-formula evaluate the logistic function exactly through simulation and prediction, so they will be closer to $-0.012$ than $-0.014$.

### What to expect from Analyses B and C

Combining the direct effect ($-0.30$ log-odds) with the opposing mediated pathway --- quitting raises BMI by $+0.90$ kg/m$^2$ on average, and each kg/m$^2$ increases log-odds of T2D by $+0.20$, contributing $+0.90 \times 0.20 = +0.18$ log-odds --- gives a net log-odds change of $-0.30 + 0.18 = -0.12$. Converting to the probability scale:

$$\Delta P_{\text{net}} \approx 0.05 \times 0.95 \times 0.12 \approx 0.006$$

The subsection below explains why the ADE is expressed as a range, then provides the full expected-value table.

### Why the ADE has a range rather than a single expected value

The ADE expected value is given as a range ($-0.010$ to $-0.014$) rather
than a single number because there are **two legitimate but different
approximation paths** to the same underlying quantity, and they give
slightly different answers.

**Path 1 — Delta method (linear approximation):** applies the first-order
Taylor expansion of the logistic function at the baseline probability $P = 0.05$:

$$\text{ADE}_{\text{delta}} \approx -P(1-P) \times |\Delta\eta|
= -0.05 \times 0.95 \times 0.30 = -0.01425 \approx -0.014$$

This uses the derivative $d\sigma/d\eta = P(1-P)$ evaluated at the
baseline log-odds $\eta_0$, and treats the logistic curve as locally
linear. It is an *upper bound* on the magnitude because the logistic
curve is concave at $P = 0.05$ — the linear approximation overshoots.

**Path 2 — Exact calculation:** evaluates the logistic function directly
at the baseline log-odds and at the shifted value:

$$\eta_0 = \log\!\left(\frac{0.05}{0.95}\right) \approx -2.944$$

$$\text{ADE}_{\text{exact}} = \sigma(\eta_0 - 0.30) - \sigma(\eta_0)
= \sigma(-3.244) - \sigma(-2.944) \approx 0.0377 - 0.0500 = -0.0123$$

This is the true value of the ADE implied by the SEM, without
approximation. The mediation package and g-formula use this exact
evaluation (through simulation and prediction from the fitted logistic
model), so the ADE they report should be close to $-0.012$, not $-0.014$.

**Why a range rather than the single exact value $-0.012$?**
The range brackets both estimates to make clear that:

1. The delta method ($-0.014$) and the exact value ($-0.012$) are both
   legitimate derivations of the same quantity — they differ only due
   to the approximation error of $\approx 0.002$.
2. The simulated ATE from the data will not be exactly $-0.012$ either,
   because the cohort has additional sources of variability (residual
   noise $\varepsilon_3 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.3^2)$ in $\text{lp\_dm}$,
   finite sample variation, subgroup heterogeneity) that shift the
   realised baseline prevalence slightly from $5\%$, which in turn
   shifts the $P(1-P)$ scaling factor.

The range $-0.010$ to $-0.014$ is therefore a **prediction interval**
for what the analysis will return, not an expression of uncertainty
about a fixed quantity. In practice any value in this range confirms
the SEM parameters are being correctly recovered.

| Quantity                        | Scale           | Derivation           | Expected value               |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Direct effect of quit           | Log-odds        | SEM coefficient      | $-0.30$ (exact)              |
| ADE (direct effect)             | Risk difference | Delta method         | $-0.014$ (upper bound)       |
| ADE (direct effect)             | Risk difference | Exact logistic       | $-0.012$ (best single value) |
| ADE prediction interval         | Risk difference | Both paths + noise   | $-0.010$ to $-0.014$         |
| Mediated effect via BMI         | Risk difference | $P(1-P) \times 0.18$ | $\approx +0.005$ to $+0.008$ |
| ATE (total effect)              | Risk difference | ADE + ACME           | $\approx -0.004$ to $-0.008$ |
| OR for quit (direct)            | Odds ratio      | $e^{-0.30}$          | $\approx 0.74$ (exact)      |
| OR for $\Delta$BMI per kg/m$^2$ | Odds ratio      | $e^{+0.20}$          | $\approx 1.22$ (exact)      |

::: callout-note
## Key takeaways on scale and the ADE range

The ADE of $\approx -0.012$ is **not** a discrepancy from the SEM's
$-0.30$ — they are the same direct effect on different scales. Comparing
$-0.012$ (risk difference) with $-0.30$ (log-odds) directly is a
category error. The OR of $e^{-0.30} \approx 0.74$ is the correct
log-odds-scale equivalent of the ADE.

The range $-0.010$ to $-0.014$ in the table above reflects two
legitimate approximation paths (delta method vs exact logistic
evaluation) plus finite-sample variability. The single best analytical
prediction is $-0.012$ from the exact calculation. Values returned by
Analyses B and C should fall within this range.
:::

## Analysis B --- Causal mediation analysis

### Statistical framework

The `mediation` package [@imai2010] implements the **potential outcomes**
decomposition of the total effect. Define $Y_i(t, m)$ as the potential
outcome for individual $i$ under treatment $T = t$ and mediator value
$M = m$. The package estimates three quantities:

$$\text{ACME}(t) = E\bigl[Y_i(t,\, M_i(1)) - Y_i(t,\, M_i(0))\bigr]$$

$$\text{ADE}(t) = E\bigl[Y_i(1,\, M_i(t)) - Y_i(0,\, M_i(t))\bigr]$$

$$\text{TE} = E\bigl[Y_i(1,\, M_i(1)) - Y_i(0,\, M_i(0))\bigr] = \text{ACME}(t) + \text{ADE}(t)$$

where $M_i(t)$ is the **potential mediator value** individual $i$ would
have under treatment $t$. The ACME (Average Causal Mediation Effect)
captures the path **Quit $\rightarrow$ $\Delta$BMI $\rightarrow$ T2D**;
the ADE (Average Direct Effect) captures the path **Quit $\rightarrow$ T2D**,
holding the mediator fixed at the value it would take under one treatment arm.

### Implementation: two-model approach

The package requires two fitted models:

**Step 1 — Mediator model** (linear, since $\Delta$BMI is continuous):

$$\Delta\text{BMI}_i = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1\,\text{Quit}_i
  + \alpha_2\,\text{BMI}_{0i} + \boldsymbol{\alpha}_c^\top \mathbf{C}_i + \varepsilon_i^M,
  \quad \varepsilon_i^M \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_M^2)$$

where $\mathbf{C}_i = (\text{Age}_i, \text{Sex}_i, \text{FamHx}_i,
\text{Alcohol}_i, \text{Activity}_i)^\top$ are pre-treatment confounders.
The key coefficient is $\hat\alpha_1$: the average BMI gain caused by quitting,
holding confounders fixed.

**Step 2 — Outcome model** (logistic, since T2D is binary):

$$\text{logit}\,P(\text{T2D}_i = 1) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{Quit}_i
  + \beta_2\,\Delta\text{BMI}_i + \boldsymbol{\beta}_c^\top \mathbf{C}_i + \varepsilon_i^Y$$

Here $\beta_1$ is the **direct effect** of quitting (log-odds scale) and
$\beta_2$ is the effect of BMI gain on T2D risk.

**Step 3 — Simulation** (`sims = 500`): for each bootstrap draw the package:

1. Draws $\hat M_i(0)$ and $\hat M_i(1)$ from the mediator model posterior
2. Plugs both into the outcome model under each treatment assignment
3. Averages the contrasts to obtain ACME and ADE on the **probability scale**

This simulation-based approach correctly handles the non-linearity of the
logistic outcome model — it does not assume effects add linearly on the
probability scale.

```{r mediation, cache=TRUE}
# Mediator model: ΔBMI ~ quit + confounders
med_model <- lm(
  delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort
)

# Outcome model: T2D ~ quit + ΔBMI + confounders
out_model <- glm(
  diabetes ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial
)

med_out <- mediate(
  med_model, out_model,
  treat    = "quit",
  mediator = "delta_bmi",
  robustSE = TRUE,
  sims     = 500
)
```

```{r mediation-results}
# Outcome model log-odds coefficients for OR conversion
out_coef <- coef(out_model)

med_tbl <- data.frame(
  Component = c("ACME (BMI-mediated effect)", "ADE (direct effect of quit)",
                "Total effect (ATE)", "Proportion mediated via BMI"),
  `Risk difference` = round(
    c(med_out$d0, med_out$z0, med_out$tau.coef, med_out$n0), 4),
  `95% CI` = c(
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", med_out$d0.ci[1],  med_out$d0.ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", med_out$z0.ci[1],  med_out$z0.ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", med_out$tau.ci[1], med_out$tau.ci[2]),
    "—"),
  `Note` = c(
    "Harmful offsetting path: BMI gain raises T2D risk",
    sprintf("OR = %.3f from outcome model log-odds = %.3f",
            exp(out_coef["quit"]), out_coef["quit"]),
    "Net effect on probability scale (ADE + ACME)",
    "Fraction of total effect operating via BMI"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(med_tbl, digits = 4,
             caption = paste0(
               "Causal mediation decomposition (Imai et al. 2010). ",
               "Risk differences are on the probability scale. ",
               "The OR for the direct effect is extracted from the ",
               "outcome model log-odds coefficient for quit."))
```

```{r mediation-plot, fig.cap="Decomposition of the total effect of quitting smoking on T2D risk into the BMI-mediated component (ACME) and the direct effect (ADE). Error bars are 95% bootstrap CIs."}
med_bar <- data.frame(
  component = factor(c("ACME\n(BMI-mediated)", "ADE\n(direct effect)"),
                     levels = c("ACME\n(BMI-mediated)", "ADE\n(direct effect)")),
  estimate  = c(med_out$d0, med_out$z0),
  lo        = c(med_out$d0.ci[1], med_out$z0.ci[1]),
  hi        = c(med_out$d0.ci[2], med_out$z0.ci[2])
)

ggplot(med_bar, aes(x = component, y = estimate, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.45, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.12, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1D9E75", "#3B8BD4")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Causal mediation: total effect decomposition",
    subtitle = sprintf("Proportion mediated via BMI: %.1f%%  |  Total ATE: %.4f",
                       med_out$n0 * 100, med_out$tau.coef),
    x = NULL, y = "Effect on P(T2D = 1)", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "none")
```

## Analysis C --- G-formula (parametric SCM)

### Statistical framework

The **g-formula** (or parametric g-computation) implements Pearl's
do-calculus directly. It computes
$E[Y(\text{do}(T=t))]$ — the mean outcome under a hypothetical intervention
that sets treatment to $t$ for everyone — rather than the conditional
expectation $E[Y \mid T=t]$ which conflates causal and selection effects.

The key insight is the **g-computation identity** for a mediator $M$ and
confounders $\mathbf{C}$:

$$E[Y(\text{do}(T=t))] =
  \int_{\mathbf{c}} \int_m
  E[Y \mid T=t,\, M=m,\, \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{c}]\;
  \underbrace{p(m \mid T=t,\, \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{c})}_{\text{mediator dist. under } do(T=t)}\;
  p(\mathbf{c})\; dm\, d\mathbf{c}$$

The crucial difference from naïve ML is the distribution over $M$:
naïve ML conditions on the **observed** $M_i$ (which was realised under the
individual's actual treatment); the g-formula integrates over the
**predicted** $M$ under the intervention value $t$. This correctly
propagates $\text{do}(\text{Quit}=1) \rightarrow \Delta\text{BMI} \uparrow
\rightarrow \text{T2D risk} \uparrow$.

### Implementation: three-step algorithm

**Step 1 — Fit the mediator model** on observed data:

$$\widehat{\Delta\text{BMI}}_i^{(t)} =
  \hat\alpha_0 + \hat\alpha_1\,t
  + \hat\alpha_2\,\text{BMI}_{0i}
  + \hat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_c^\top \mathbf{C}_i$$

For each individual, predict $\Delta$BMI *as if* $\text{Quit} = t$,
regardless of their observed treatment. This is the operationalisation
of $\text{do}(\text{Quit} = t)$ in the mediator equation.

**Step 2 — Predict T2D risk using the counterfactual mediator**:

$$\hat P_i^{(t)} = \sigma\!\left(
  \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1\,t
  + \hat\beta_2\,\widehat{\Delta\text{BMI}}_i^{(t)}
  + \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_c^\top \mathbf{C}_i\right)$$

**Step 3 — Average over the covariate distribution** (standardisation):

$$\widehat{\text{ATE}} =
  \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat P_i^{(1)}
  - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat P_i^{(0)}$$

This is a **Monte Carlo approximation** of the population-level
do-calculus integral, using the observed covariate distribution as
the reference population. The bootstrap CI re-runs all three steps
on each resample to propagate uncertainty from both models.

**Why this differs from naïve ML:** Naïve ML predicts
$E[\text{T2D} \mid \text{Quit}=1, \Delta\text{BMI} = \Delta\text{BMI}_i^{\text{obs}}]$
— it plugs in the *observed* BMI change for each individual, which was
determined under their actual (not counterfactual) treatment. A quitter
who happened to gain little weight gets a low predicted risk; a hypothetical
non-quitter who would have gained weight anyway is never considered.
The g-formula instead asks: *if this individual were assigned to quit,
what BMI change would we predict, and what T2D risk would follow?*

```{r gformula, cache=TRUE}
med_gform <- lm(
  delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort
)
out_gform <- glm(
  diabetes ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial
)

gformula_ate <- function(df, treat_val) {
  df_int           <- df
  df_int$quit      <- treat_val
  df_int$delta_bmi <- predict(med_gform, newdata = df_int)
  mean(predict(out_gform, newdata = df_int, type = "response"))
}

p_dm_quit  <- gformula_ate(cohort, 1)
p_dm_smoke <- gformula_ate(cohort, 0)
ate_gform  <- p_dm_quit - p_dm_smoke

# Bootstrap 95% CI
set.seed(42)
boot_ate <- replicate(500, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(cohort), replace = TRUE)
  b   <- cohort[idx, ]
  m   <- lm(delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity, data = b)
  o   <- glm(diabetes  ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
             data = b, family = binomial)
  f   <- function(tv) {
    d <- b; d$quit <- tv; d$delta_bmi <- predict(m, newdata = d)
    mean(predict(o, newdata = d, type = "response"))
  }
  f(1) - f(0)
})
ci_gform <- quantile(boot_ate, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

```{r gformula-results}
# OR approximation from the outcome model used in the g-formula
out_gform_coef <- coef(out_gform)
or_direct_gform <- exp(out_gform_coef["quit"])
or_bmi_gform    <- exp(out_gform_coef["delta_bmi"])

# Risk ratio approximation: P(T2D|do(quit=1)) / P(T2D|do(quit=0))
rr_gform <- p_dm_quit / p_dm_smoke

gform_tbl <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "P(T2D = 1 | do(quit=1))",
    "P(T2D = 1 | do(quit=0))",
    "ATE  [do(quit=1) − do(quit=0)]",
    "95% bootstrap CI",
    "Risk ratio  [do(quit=1) / do(quit=0)]",
    "OR for quit (log-odds, outcome model)",
    "OR for ΔBMI per 1 kg/m² (outcome model)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    sprintf("%.4f", p_dm_quit),
    sprintf("%.4f", p_dm_smoke),
    sprintf("%.4f", ate_gform),
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", ci_gform[1], ci_gform[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f", rr_gform),
    sprintf("%.3f  (log-odds = %.3f)", or_direct_gform, out_gform_coef["quit"]),
    sprintf("%.3f  (log-odds = %.3f)", or_bmi_gform,    out_gform_coef["delta_bmi"])
  ),
  Interpretation = c(
    "Predicted T2D probability if everyone quits (BMI allowed to rise)",
    "Predicted T2D probability if no one quits",
    "Causal risk difference — net effect on probability scale",
    "Bootstrap percentile interval for ATE",
    "Relative risk — quitters vs non-quitters under do-calculus",
    "Direct protective effect of quitting; OR < 1 = protective",
    "Harmful effect of each kg/m² BMI gain; OR > 1 = harmful"
  )
)
knitr::kable(gform_tbl,
  caption = paste0(
    "G-formula results. The ATE is on the probability (risk difference) scale. ",
    "ORs are from the outcome model and are on the log-odds scale — ",
    "they cannot be directly compared to the ATE but show the direction and ",
    "magnitude of each pathway before the offsetting effects are combined."))
```

## Naïve vs causal ATE comparison

```{r ate-comparison}
naive_pred_quit  <- mean(predict(naive_fit,
  newdata = transform(cohort, quit = 1), type = "response"))
naive_pred_smoke <- mean(predict(naive_fit,
  newdata = transform(cohort, quit = 0), type = "response"))
ate_naive <- naive_pred_quit - naive_pred_smoke

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Method   = c("Naïve ML (biased — conditions on mediator)",
                 "G-formula (causal — propagates quit → ΔBMI → T2D)",
                 "Absolute bias"),
    ATE = round(c(ate_naive, ate_gform, abs(ate_naive - ate_gform)), 4)
  ),
  caption = "Naïve vs causal ATE: the bias introduced by ignoring the smoking → BMI pathway"
)
```

```{r scatter-plot, fig.cap="Individual-level naïve vs causal predicted T2D risk for quitters. Points above the 45° line (dashed) are patients for whom causal reasoning gives a *higher* risk estimate than naïve ML — correctly accounting for the BMI gain caused by quitting. Red colour indicates higher baseline BMI."}
cohort$risk_naive <- predict(naive_fit, type = "response")

tmp_q1           <- cohort; tmp_q1$quit <- 1
tmp_q1$delta_bmi <- predict(med_gform, newdata = tmp_q1)
cohort$risk_causal_quit <- predict(out_gform, newdata = tmp_q1, type = "response")

quitters <- cohort[cohort$quit == 1, ]

ggplot(quitters, aes(x = risk_naive, y = risk_causal_quit, colour = bmi0)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.9) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#333") +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#3B8BD4", high = "#D85A30", name = "Baseline BMI") +
  labs(
    title    = "Naïve ML vs causal (g-formula) T2D risk — quitters only",
    subtitle = "Points above diagonal: causal model gives higher risk\n(propagates quit → BMI gain → diabetes)",
    x = "Naïve ML predicted risk  [conditions on observed post-BMI]",
    y = "Causal predicted risk  [do(quit=1), propagates ΔBMI]"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

## Heterogeneous treatment effects (CATE)

@feuerriegel2024 emphasise **conditional** ATE (CATE). The claim that high-BMI patients face a larger short-term T2D risk increase from quitting rests on two links in the SEM that must both be visible in the data:

1.  **High baseline BMI predicts more post-cessation weight gain** --- encoded in the mediator equation as `0.15 * (bmi0 - 23) * quit`. A patient at BMI = 30 is expected to gain $0.15 \times 7 = 1.05$ kg/m² *extra* compared to a patient at BMI = 23.
2.  **Greater weight gain increases T2D risk** --- encoded as `+0.20 * bmi_post` in the outcome equation.

We verify link (1) directly from the mediator model before computing the full CATE, so the mechanism is transparent rather than implicit.

### Step 1 --- Verify: predicted ΔBMI by BMI group under do(quit = 1)

```{r cate-mediator}
cohort$bmi_grp <- cut(
  bmi0,
  breaks = c(-Inf, 22, 25, 28, Inf),
  labels = c("< 22", "22-25", "25-28", ">= 28")
)

# Predict counterfactual ΔBMI under do(quit=1) for each individual,
# then average within BMI group — using the already-fitted med_gform
med_check <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(cohort$bmi_grp), function(g) {
  sub      <- cohort[cohort$bmi_grp == g, ]
  d1       <- sub; d1$quit <- 1
  d0       <- sub; d0$quit <- 0
  dbmi_q1  <- predict(med_gform, newdata = d1)
  dbmi_q0  <- predict(med_gform, newdata = d0)
  data.frame(
    `BMI group`           = g,
    n                     = nrow(sub),
    `Mean ΔBMI (smokers)` = round(mean(dbmi_q0), 3),
    `Mean ΔBMI (quitters)`= round(mean(dbmi_q1), 3),
    `Extra gain from quitting` = round(mean(dbmi_q1) - mean(dbmi_q0), 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))

knitr::kable(med_check,
  caption = paste0(
    "Predicted post-cessation ΔBMI by baseline BMI group under the g-formula. ",
    "The 'extra gain from quitting' column increases monotonically with BMI group, ",
    "confirming that the BMI x quit interaction in the mediator model is operating ",
    "as intended."))
```

### Step 2 --- CATE from the full g-formula

```{r cate}
cate_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(cohort$bmi_grp), function(g) {
  sub <- cohort[cohort$bmi_grp == g, ]
  if (nrow(sub) < 30) return(NULL)
  m  <- lm(delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity, data = sub)
  o  <- glm(diabetes  ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
            data = sub, family = binomial)
  f  <- function(tv) {
    d <- sub; d$quit <- tv; d$delta_bmi <- predict(m, newdata = d)
    mean(predict(o, newdata = d, type = "response"))
  }
  p1 <- f(1); p0 <- f(0)
  data.frame(bmi_grp = g, n = nrow(sub),
             p_smoke = round(p0, 4),
             p_quit  = round(p1, 4),
             cate    = round(p1 - p0, 4))
}))

knitr::kable(cate_df,
  col.names = c("BMI group", "n", "P(T2D | do(quit=0))",
                "P(T2D | do(quit=1))", "CATE"),
  caption = paste0(
    "CATE by baseline BMI group (g-formula). ",
    "A positive CATE means quitting increases short-term T2D risk in that group. ",
    "Note that differences in baseline T2D risk across BMI groups (p_smoke column) ",
    "affect the absolute CATE even when the log-odds effect is similar, ",
    "because P(1-P) varies — see Section on scale interpretation."))
```

::: callout-warning
## Interpreting the CATE table carefully

The CATE values reflect **both** the treatment heterogeneity of interest (BMI-mediated extra weight gain) **and** differences in baseline T2D prevalence across BMI groups (which changes the $P(1-P)$ scaling factor even for the same log-odds effect). A large negative CATE in the $\geq 28$ group does not necessarily mean quitting is more beneficial there --- it may simply reflect higher baseline T2D risk in that group, which amplifies all effects on the probability scale.

The mediator table in Step 1 is therefore the cleaner test of the heterogeneity claim: if "extra gain from quitting" increases monotonically across BMI groups, the mechanism is confirmed regardless of the probability-scale CATE pattern.
:::

```{r cate-plot, fig.cap="CATE by BMI group. A positive bar (red) means quitting increases short-term T2D risk in that group via weight gain. The pattern should be interpreted alongside the mediator table above."}
cate_df$bmi_grp <- factor(cate_df$bmi_grp, levels = levels(cohort$bmi_grp))

ggplot(cate_df, aes(x = bmi_grp, y = cate, fill = cate < 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#D85A30", "TRUE" = "#1D9E75"),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "Quitting increases T2D risk (short-term)",
               "TRUE"  = "Quitting reduces T2D risk")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "CATE by baseline BMI group (g-formula)",
    subtitle = paste0("The CATE pattern reflects both treatment heterogeneity",
                      " and baseline T2D risk differences across groups.\n",
                      "See mediator table for the cleaner test of the BMI-gain mechanism."),
    x    = "Baseline BMI group (kg/m²)",
    y    = "CATE: P(T2D | do(quit=1)) - P(T2D | do(quit=0))",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Summary

```{r summary-table}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Finding = c(
      "Naïve ML ATE (biased)",
      "G-formula ATE (causal)",
      "Absolute bias",
      "Proportion of total effect mediated via ΔBMI",
      "Direct protective effect of quitting (ADE)"
    ),
    Value = c(
      sprintf("%.4f", ate_naive),
      sprintf("%.4f  [95%% CI: %.4f, %.4f]", ate_gform, ci_gform[1], ci_gform[2]),
      sprintf("%.4f", abs(ate_naive - ate_gform)),
      sprintf("%.1f%%", med_out$n0 * 100),
      sprintf("%.4f  [95%% CI: %.4f, %.4f]", med_out$z0,
              med_out$z0.ci[1], med_out$z0.ci[2])
    )
  ),
  caption = "Key results"
)
```

::: callout-note
## Key takeaway

Naïve ML implicitly assumes BMI is unaffected by the treatment decision. The g-formula correctly propagates `do(quit=1)` through the mediator ΔBMI, giving a different --- and causally valid --- population-average risk prediction. The mediator model confirms that higher-BMI patients gain more weight after quitting (Step 1 in the CATE section), which is the mechanism driving treatment heterogeneity. The CATE table on the probability scale must be interpreted carefully because baseline T2D risk differences across BMI groups affect absolute CATEs independently of the treatment effect --- the mediator table provides the cleaner evidence for the heterogeneity claim.
:::
